name: Ilyushin Il-76MD 'Gajraj'

header.one_liner: The IAF's Russian-origin heavy-lift airlifter (~17 acquired 1985–89, ~11–14 flyable), locally named 'Gajraj'; it is also the base airframe for India's Il-78MKI tankers and A-50EI Phalcon AWACS. Ageing D-30KP engines and Russia-Ukraine supply strain are driving a life-extension/re-engine (PS-90) study toward the 2040s.

header.mobility_or_class: Four-engine strategic heavy-lift jet transport (~40+ t payload)

what_it_is.prose: The Ilyushin Il-76MD, locally named 'Gajraj', is the Indian Air Force's Russian-origin four-engine strategic heavy-lift airlifter, acquired between 1985 and 1989 (about 17 aircraft) and flown by No. 25 Squadron 'Himalayan Eagles' at Chandigarh. It carries in excess of 40 tonnes and is powered by four Soloviev/Aviadvigatel D-30KP turbofans. Beyond pure airlift, the Il-76 airframe is strategically important as the base platform for two of India's most valuable force-multipliers: the six Il-78MKI aerial-refuelling tankers and the three A-50EI 'Phalcon' AWACS (an Israeli EL/W-2090 Phalcon radar on a Russian Il-76 airframe). Reported fleet numbers vary — around 17 acquired, with roughly 11 to 14 flyable at various points as aircraft are decommissioned or cannibalised for spares; at least two have been grounded at Chandigarh since 2022. The fleet's core problem is its ageing D-30KP engines and, since the Russia-Ukraine war, disrupted spares and overhaul support. India approved a modernisation programme (avionics and engines) via the Defence Acquisition Council around 2015 (reported at roughly ₹4,250 crore / $650 million) and has since studied re-engining with the more efficient Aviadvigatel PS-90A-76 turbofan, glass-cockpit avionics and secure indigenous communications, working increasingly with domestic firms rather than relying solely on Russian state entities. The aim is to keep a core fleet of about ten Il-76 flying into the 2040s, with structural life-extension studies examining feasibility beyond 2050. Serviceability has been a persistent concern, with availability reported to have fallen as low as around 32%.

deployments_procurement.summary: India acquired ~17 Il-76MD 'Gajraj' from the USSR/Russia in 1985–89, operating them from Chandigarh; the airframe also underpins the Il-78MKI tankers and A-50EI Phalcon AWACS. Ageing D-30KP engines and Russia-Ukraine spares strain have pushed a DAC-approved modernisation (~$650M, 2015) and a PS-90 re-engine study to sustain a core fleet into the 2040s.

import_dependencies.summary: The Il-76 and its tanker/AWACS derivatives are deeply dependent on Russia (Ilyushin design authority, D-30KP engines, TAPO overhaul) — support strained by the Russia-Ukraine war — plus Israel for the A-50EI's Phalcon radar.

items.note: Ilyushin / Tashkent (Russia/ex-USSR) — original design house; overhaul historically in Russia, now strained.
Aviadvigatel (Russia) — ageing D-30KP powerplant and spares; re-engine option is again a Russian engine.
Russia-Ukraine war has cut spares; cannibalisation and groundings have pushed availability as low as ~32%.
Israel (IAI/ELTA EL/W-2090 Phalcon) mounted on the Russian Il-76 airframe — a tri-national dependency.

Defence Acquisition Council approves ~$650M Il-76 engine and avionics modernisation.
At least two Il-76 grounded at Chandigarh amid Russia-Ukraine spares disruption.
IAF studies deep upgrade with PS-90A-76 re-engine and domestic firms to sustain the fleet toward the 2040s.

faq.question: How many Il-76 does the IAF operate and what is 'Gajraj'?
faq.answer: 'Gajraj' is the IAF's local name for its Ilyushin Il-76MD heavy-lift transports, acquired from the USSR/Russia between 1985 and 1989 (about 17 aircraft) and flown by No. 25 Squadron at Chandigarh. Reported flyable numbers vary between roughly 11 and 14 as aircraft are decommissioned or cannibalised for spares, with at least two grounded since 2022.

faq.question: Why is the Il-76 airframe strategically important beyond airlift?
faq.answer: The Il-76 is the base platform for two of India's key force-multipliers: the six Il-78MKI aerial-refuelling tankers and the three A-50EI 'Phalcon' AWACS, which mount an Israeli EL/W-2090 Phalcon radar on a Russian Il-76 airframe. That makes the Il-76 line central not just to strategic heavy lift but to India's air-to-air refuelling and airborne early-warning capabilities.

faq.question: What is being done about the ageing Il-76 fleet and its engines?
faq.answer: India approved a modernisation of engines and avionics via the Defence Acquisition Council around 2015 (reported at roughly ₹4,250 crore / $650 million) and has studied re-engining with the more efficient Aviadvigatel PS-90A-76 turbofan plus glass-cockpit avionics and indigenous communications, increasingly with domestic firms. The goal is to keep a core fleet of about ten Il-76 flying into the 2040s, with feasibility beyond 2050 under study, despite Russia-Ukraine-related spares shortages that have cut serviceability sharply.
